newsitem.title: USA: Replace the eagle on the quarter? It could happen.
newsitem.headline: Replace the eagle on the quarter? It could happen.

text.p: Could the eagle be replaced by New York's Empire State building on the back of the quarter? Or by California's state symbol, the bear?
Conceivably, yes, under a programme endorsed Friday by the U.S. Treasury to permit each of the 50 states to come up with their own design for the back of a commemorative quarter.
The special coins could be in circulation by early 1999, after being screened by a committee to make sure they were suitably serious.

Thus, a famous figure from history might appear on the back of the quarter in the future, or some historic site, but it is unlikely quarters wil carry images of popular figures like basketball superstar Michael Jordan.

With an apparent tinge of reluctance, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin confirmed the U.S. Mint was prepared to issue special commemorative quarters if Congress passed legislation instructing it to do so.

Rubin's agreement to a programme under which the 50 states could have commemorative quarters in circulation came in a letter to the chairman of the House Subcommittee on Domestic and International Monetary Policy, Michael Castle, a Delaware Repuplican and a force in the effort to have them issued.

"If Congress directs us to proceed with the 50 State Commemorative Quarter Programme, the Department of the Treasury stands ready to do it," Rubin said in a letter to Castle in which he mentioned a few personal misgivings about the idea.

The Treasury Secretary noted a specially commissioned study found "a large percentage of people who are indifferent to the programme or are unfavourably disposed toward it" along with "a substantial degree of interest" in it.

"For this reason I am concerned that this programme could affect the public's perception of our coinage," Rubin said, adding he wanted any legislative directive to include provisions for a design review with final approval made by the Treasury secretary.
"This process will ensure that no frivolous or inappropriate designs are adopted," Rubin said.

Castle said he intended to bring legislation before Congress "as soon as possible" telling Treasury to start issuing commemorative quarters. The earliest they are likely to be jingling in taxpayers' pockets -- or squirreled away by collectors -- is early 1999.

The plan is to issue the commemorative coins at the rate of five a year, so the programme would last 10 years until all 50 states had their coins in circulation. Then the Mint would revert to placing the eagle on the back of all quarters.
There has not been a commemorative quarter placed into circulation since the 1975-76 Bicentennial two-bit piece, which had George Washington in the usual place but a drummer boy on the back.
The last real change in coinage came in 1979, when the multi-sided Susan B. Anthony $1 coin was introduced to honour the 19th century suffragette.

The Susan B. Anthony dollar is no longer being minted but is in circulation, frequently offered as change by U.S. Post Offices vending machines -- partly because the Mint has a stockpile of them as many people spurned the coin because they felt it looked and felt too much like a quarter.
